usage: I have a reservation (just so you know)
Polite; said as you walk in to check in
반말, only telling a friend, never the staff
Formal 합쇼체, upscale salon or sounding crisp
I didn't book — is it possible (to walk in)?
The walk-in version when you have no booking

Hi, I have a reservation.
The standard check-in line right after greeting
세 시에 예약했는데요. 이름은 김민수예요.
I booked for three o'clock — the name is Kim Minsu.
Add the time and name so they find your booking
저기요, 네이버로 예약했는데요. 확인 좀 해 주세요.
Excuse me, I booked through Naver — could you check?
네이버 예약 (Naver booking) is how most Koreans reserve salons

usage: Polite; declaring you only want a haircut
반말, to a friend, not to the stylist
I would like just a cut
I'd like to get my hair cut
Softer way to open with what you came for
examples: 오늘은 커트만 할게요.
Today I'll just get a cut.
오늘은 ('today') frames it as today's choice
펌은 안 하고 커트만 할게요.
No perm — just a cut, please.
Contrast 안 하다 (not doing) with what you do want
커트만 할게요. 얼마예요?
Just a cut, please — how much is it?
Pair with 얼마예요 to confirm the price upfront
nuance: 커트만 할게요 is 커트 (the loanword 'cut') + -만 ('only') + 할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 form of 하다, announcing your own intention politely). The -만 is doing the real work: it tells the stylist you want ONLY a haircut and no extras like perm or dye, which matters because salons often upsell or assume add-ons. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the friendly customer register — polite but not stiff. Note the spelling/sound: Koreans write and say 커트 for a haircut (헤어컷 also appears in menus), and the verb is 머리(를) 자르다 ('to cut hair') in everyday speech — so 커트하다 and 머리 자르다 are interchangeable, with 커트 sounding more salon-technical. The dividing line from 머리 자르려고요 ('I came to get a cut') is that 커트만 할게요 actively EXCLUDES other services via 만, while 자르려고요 just states your purpose. The English-speaker trap is putting 만 in the wrong slot or using the wrong verb: saying 커트 할게요만 is broken word order (만 attaches to the noun: 커트만), and translating 'just' as 그냥 (그냥 커트 할게요) means 'just casually a cut', a different nuance. Also don't confuse 커트 with 컷 used for editing/film; for hair it's 커트.

english: Just tidy it up / trim it, please
usage: Polite; light cleanup, not a big change
반말, to a friend cutting your hair
Could you tidy it up, please?
끝만 살짝 ('only the tips, slightly') for a tiny trim
examples: 길이는 그대로, 다듬어만 주세요.
Keep the length — just tidy it up.
길이는 그대로 ('length as is') signals no real shortening
끝이 좀 상했어요. 다듬어 주세요.
The ends are a bit damaged — please trim them.
상하다 ('to be damaged') gives the reason for a trim
많이 자르지 말고 그냥 다듬어 주세요.
Don't cut much — just tidy it up.
많이 자르지 말고 ('without cutting much') protects your length
nuance: 다듬어 주세요 is 다듬다 ('to trim, neaten, tidy up') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form ('please do for me'). This is the single most useful salon word for someone who does NOT want a dramatic change: 다듬다 means cleaning up the shape and trimming the ends while keeping essentially the same length and style. The crucial contrast is with 자르다 ('to cut'): 자르다 implies actually shortening / removing length, while 다듬다 implies light maintenance — if you say 잘라 주세요 the stylist may take off more than you wanted, so for 'just a trim' always reach for 다듬다. To be extra safe, stack 끝만 살짝 ('just the tips, lightly') or 많이 자르지 말고 ('without cutting much'). The English-speaker trap is exactly this verb choice — 'trim' gets mistranslated as 자르다, producing a real haircut when you wanted maintenance. Another pitfall is the irregular conjugation: 다듬다 keeps the ㅁ, so it's 다듬어 (not 다듬워 or 다듬아); and the favor form needs 주세요 — bare 다듬으세요 would oddly command the stylist to trim their OWN hair. Register stays 존댓말 with staff.

english: Please don't make it too short
usage: Please don't make it too short
Polite; capping how short they go
반말, to a friend cutting it
Please don't make it too long
The opposite, when you want it shorter
examples: 앞은 괜찮은데 옆은 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요.
The front's fine, but don't make the sides too short.
Aim the limit at one area: 옆 ('the sides')
저번에 너무 짧게 잘라서, 이번엔 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요.
Last time it was cut too short, so this time please not too short.
저번에 … 잘라서 ('last time [they] cut it …, so') explains why you're cautious
귀는 덮을 정도로, 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요.
Long enough to cover the ears — not too short, please.
귀를 덮다 ('cover the ears') gives a concrete length cue
nuance: 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 is 너무 ('too') + 짧다 ('to be short') in the -지 않게 form ('in a way that is NOT…') + 해 주세요 ('please make it'). The structure -지 않게 해 주세요 = 'please make it so that it's not ~', a hugely useful frame for setting limits on any service. Here it caps the haircut: cut, but don't overshoot into 'too short'. The natural alternative is 너무 짧게 자르지 마세요 ('don't cut it too short') with the prohibitive -지 마세요 — both are correct; the -지 않게 version softens by describing the desired result, while -지 마세요 directly forbids the action. The English-speaker trap is the double-negative word order: learners produce 너무 안 짧게 (wrong placement of 안) or 짧지 않게 너무, scrambling it — the fixed order is 너무 + 짧지 않게. Another pitfall is using 작다 ('small in size') instead of 짧다 ('short in length') — hair is 짧다, never 작다. Also 너무 literally skews negative ('excessively'), so it fits perfectly with limits; don't replace it with 많이 ('a lot') here, since 많이 짧지 않게 sounds off. Keep 해 주세요 to make it a request to the stylist, not a self-command.

Using 작다 instead of 짧다 for hair.

Dropping 해 주세요 and saying just 너무 짧지 않게.

english: Please give me bangs / keep the bangs down
usage: Polite; asking for front fringe forward
반말, to a friend styling your hair
The opposite: 까다, swept off the forehead
Please trim my bangs a bit
examples: 앞머리 있는 게 좋아서 내려 주세요.
I like having bangs, so please keep them down.
있는 게 좋다 ('prefer having') states your preference
앞머리 내려 주시고, 눈썹 정도 길이로 해 주세요.
Bangs down, please, and about eyebrow length.
눈썹 정도 길이 ('about eyebrow length') sets the cut line
원래 앞머리 까는데, 오늘은 한번 내려 볼까 해요.
I usually push my bangs back, but today I'm thinking of trying them down.
까다 vs. 내리다 contrast, with -아 볼까 해요 ('thinking of trying')
nuance: 앞머리 내려 주세요 is 앞머리 ('front hair / bangs / fringe', lit. 'front-head') + 내리다 ('to lower, bring down') in the favor form. 앞머리 is the fixed Korean word for the fringe over your forehead, and 내리다 means to wear it DOWN over the forehead (as opposed to swept back). The essential contrast is 까다: 앞머리(를) 까다 means to push the bangs UP/BACK off the forehead — so 내려 주세요 (down/forward) and 까 주세요 (back/up) are opposites you must not swap, since they produce completely different looks. The English-speaker trap starts with the vocabulary: there is no single word 'bangs' in their head-to-Korean map, so they describe it ('the hair in front') and confuse the stylist; just learn 앞머리. Another pitfall is the verb — learners reach for 자르다 thinking 'bangs = cut bangs', but 내리다 is about how you WEAR them, and to actually create/trim bangs you'd say 앞머리 만들어 주세요 ('make bangs') or 앞머리 다듬어 주세요 ('trim the bangs'). Also note 머리 alone means 'head/hair' generally; the front fringe specifically is 앞머리. Keep 존댓말 with the stylist.

english: Please make it like this photo
usage: Please make it like this photo
Could it turn out like this photo?
Asking if the look is achievable for you
examples: 이 사진처럼 해 주세요. 가능해요?
Make it like this photo, please — is it possible?
Follow with 가능해요 to check feasibility
이 사진처럼 하고 싶은데, 제 머리로 될까요?
I want it like this photo — would it work with my hair?
제 머리로 될까요 ('work with my hair') asks realistically
이 사진처럼 자연스럽게 해 주세요.
Please make it natural like this photo.
Add 자연스럽게 ('naturally') to guide the vibe
nuance: 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 is 이 사진 ('this photo') + -처럼 ('like, as') + 해 주세요 ('please do it for me'). Showing a reference photo is the single most reliable way to communicate a hairstyle across a language gap, and -처럼 ('like ~') is the particle that attaches to the noun to mean 'in the manner of this photo'. The key grammar point is that -처럼 fuses directly onto the noun with no spacing issues: 사진처럼, never 사진 같이 처럼 or 사진를 처럼. A close synonym is 사진같이 (사진 + 같이, 'same as the photo'), which is also natural; -처럼 and 같이 are near-interchangeable here, with -처럼 feeling a touch more standard in this request. The English-speaker trap is over-building the sentence with the verb 보이다 ('to look') — saying 이 사진처럼 보이게 해 주세요 ('make it LOOK like this photo') is understandable but wordier than natives need; plain 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 is what people say. Another pitfall is forgetting to actually verify realism, so Koreans often append 가능해요? or 될까요? ('is it possible?') because a photo of someone else's hair may not suit yours. Keep 존댓말; the favor verb 해 주세요 keeps it a polite request, not a command.

english: Please keep it similar to my hair now
usage: Keep it similar to my hair now
Keep it like it is now
그대로 ('as is') for no change in style
examples: 크게 바꾸지 말고 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요.
Nothing drastic — keep it similar to my hair now.
크게 바꾸지 말고 ('without big changes') sets the limit

길이만 줄이다 ('only shorten the length') refines it

The #1 English-speaker trap: 'I don't like it' must be 마음에 안 들어요, not 안 좋아해요. Another pitfall is the particle in the idiom: it's 마음'에' 들다 (locative 에), so never 마음을 들다 or 마음이 안 들다.

mistakes: Saying 이거 안 좋아해요 to mean 'I don't like this haircut'.
좋아하다 is for general liking of people/activities. For not liking a result, use the idiom 마음에 안 들어요.
Getting the particle wrong: 마음을 안 들어요 or 마음이 안 들어요.
The idiom takes locative 에: 마음에 안 들어요 ('it doesn't enter my heart'). Not 을/를 or 이/가 on 마음.
Demanding a redo bluntly: 다시 하세요.
다시 하세요 is a command and sounds rude to staff. Ask as an ability question with honorific 시: 다시 해 주실 수 있어요?, and lead with 죄송한데.
